questions.title: Does the Fifth Circuit's refusal to certify ambiguous statutory terms to the Louisiana Supreme Court violate Erie doctrine principles regarding state law uncertainty?
questions.question_body: In this opinion, the plaintiffs explicitly asked the Fifth Circuit to certify questions of statutory interpretation to the Louisiana Supreme Court regarding 'receipt' and 'certification.' The court declined, citing *Jefferson v. Lead Indus. Ass'n*, stating that a mere lack of state supreme court precedent isn't enough. However, since Louisiana courts demand 'strict adherence' to this statute and even small defects invalidate cancellations (*Eaglin*), isn't there a strong argument that true ambiguity exists? How does the appellate court balance its duty to predict state law accurately against its reluctance to use certification when the stakes involve invalidating insurance coverage?

questions.title: Can an automated email trigger a statutory 'receipt' requirement for policy cancellation before any human agent at the insurer sees the document?
questions.question_body: The core factual dispute here is timing: GoAuto's computer system receives an API call/email from APAC and immediately cancels the policy, while a human employee doesn't physically handle or sign the paperwork until hours later. The court ruled that an automated web service interaction counts as 'receipt' under La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i). Does this interpretation align with traditional agency principles where 'receipt' implies actual knowledge by an authorized representative? Is it legally sound to say an insurer has 'taken possession' of a legal notice when only its server acknowledged it, especially given the strict liability nature of these statutes?

questions.title: Is a corporate entity capable of 'certifying' facts under La. R.S. 9:3550 without an individual employee signing or identifying themselves on the notice?
questions.question_body: The Plaintiffs argued that because no specific employee signed or was named on APAC's cancellation notice, there was no valid 'certification' required by the statute. The court rejected this, noting that the statute says 'the insurance premium finance company' certifies, not an individual. Given that *Benitez* suggested missing signatures could be fatal if other elements weren't met, how does this decision reconcile with general evidence rules requiring authentication? Doesn't allowing unsigned, anonymous corporate certifications undermine the purpose of 'strict adherence,' which is meant to ensure clarity and accountability in cancellation dates?

questions.title: How does the concept of 'strict adherence' functionally differ from 'substantial compliance' in Louisiana insurance premium finance cases post-*Williams v. GoAuto*?
questions.question_body: The opinion repeatedly cites Louisiana precedents demanding 'strict adherence' to cancellation procedures, noting that '[a]ny defect... results in an ineffective cancellation.' Yet, in upholding GoAuto's process (where signatures happen after cancellation and humans aren't involved initially), the court seems to allow deviations from literalistic interpretations (like requiring a pre-cancellation signature). If 'strict adherence' is indeed absolute as stated in *Delatte*, why didn't these technical gaps constitute defects? Did *Williams* effectively lower the bar from strict literalism to functional compliance for modern digital processes?

questions.title: What is the procedural significance of dismissing claims with prejudice versus dismissal without prejudice in summary judgment rulings based on statutory compliance?
questions.question_body: The district court dismissed all claims against GoAuto with prejudice after granting summary judgment on statutory compliance grounds. In my reading, if GoAuto's procedure was merely technically compliant but arguably unfair or misleading (as alleged by plaintiffs regarding misrepresentation), shouldn't there be room for further discovery on bad faith claims separate from pure statutory construction? Why did the appellate court affirm a dismissal with prejudice when the underlying issue was purely about interpreting whether their automation software met a state statute? Does this prevent plaintiffs from ever re-litigating whether those specific procedures caused them harm?
